You meet people coming the other way, so if you do decide to go, you might choose to go at the beginning or the end of the day because there is not much room on the stairs. Sturdy, rubber soled shoes are a must and it would be helpful to wear a hat because dripping muddy water frequently assaults your hair and clothes. Bed mattresses are very hard,  which i know suit Asian tastes,  but many westerners prefer a softer mattress,  including me.   The staff were pleasant,  and were very helpful with late night food. The restaurant has a very good breakfast with a lot of choice, not all perfect,  but certainly plenty of options that allows you to find something you love. Nepal is poor,  as are the staff and workers. This is reflected in some of the "rough at the edges" handling of inappropriate customers and management of unusual situations.   The Nepalese people are so polite and nice to visitors, maybe not always logical, unfortunately the same can not be said of some visitor's, with their rude crude attitudes directed at the Nepali staff.   Given what they must deal with,  i have a lot of respect for their continued willingness to serve.  The hotel is a historical palace, but was severely damaged during the 2015 earthquake,  but has remained open using the undamaged part of the hotel,  while the damaged part is slowly repaired .  We were two couples staying 2 nights then another night a few days later.  I am neutral on this hotel,  but i do note it certainly works as a convenient transit hotel when you visit kathmandu enroute to somewhere else.  It is nicely priced!

This is the neatest corner of Kathmandu. The gardens are well-maintained. There are terraces, benches, shade and sunny spots, a number of ponds and fountains. Overall, a wonderful place to go to if you're in need of some peace and quiet, or when you've had an overdose of the dust and dirt and noise of Kathmandu.

The security guard at the gate needs additional training in English. He refused to let us enter the garden after we had paid, and couldn't explain why. Turns out he thought we were part of another group who were still busy paying, and even though we told him that we had already paid, he just said, "Excuse me, don't go there." When the next group came through, he took their tickets and scanned it, and then when we gave him our tickets, he scanned it and allowed us to enter. He never asked for our tickets, and as we had not been here before, how could we know that this was their system?

One more point: You are not allowed to bring a picnic to this garden. According to their website, you may bring snacks, but not a picnic. If you want to eat, you are welcome to dine at the Kaiser Café, and although it seems to be an excellent restaurant, it's not suitable for families with small children, and its menu isn't budget-friendly.

Now, if i have to pay Rs300 to walk through a garden too small to be called a park, and aren't allowed to bring my own food, then i'm going to call it expensive. Of course, as with everything else in Nepal, foreigners pay more than locals.

When we arrived we were given a room facing the back, not the gardens.  It was dark and charmless.  Worst of all it didn't look like it had been cleaned in quite a while. Perhaps it had something to do with the fact that the mountains came out the next day - amazing!

The breakfast was fine, the gardens pretty and pool was great for our little ones.  The location is good, walking distance to the lake and shopping.  They do also serve the nicest Nepali Tea we had while on our trip.

One final thing though. I did lose a necklace while we were staying here.  I can't be 100% exactly sure what day but I am sure I had it when we arrived and I didn't wear it, but it was gone when we got back to Katmandu. I mentioned it to the hotel but they seemed really unconcerned. Not great service.

In our first room we could not sleep as pipes kept making squeaky noises all night which woke us up. Also we were right by the stairs which creaked loudly when other guests used them, which also woke us up and one of the (very hard) beds made really loud squeaky noises when you made any movement at all, which also  kept waking us up. We asked to move rooms because of the problems and the staff were very nice about it and let us switch. 

However, we were then put into a room which backed onto another property which plays VERY loud jazz at night! We were also woken up by a cleaner vacuuming the carpet outside our room at 5:45am one morning. Don't accept one of these rooms, especially if it is hot, as the air con unit us downstairs and you can't feel it upstairs where the beds are, meaning it is very hot and sweaty in bed. Also, the ceilings are very low and you can hear EVERYTHING going in in the bathroom of the room above you! We lay awake at night listening to people use the toilet seemingly right over our heads! We're not especially sensitive to noise, my husband is actually hearing impaired and he was still bothered by these noise problems! 

The pool area is lovely, but be warned that although you will be paying quite a lot of money to stay there and hope for a peaceful swim, the hotel let anyone pay a small price to use the facilities. He did put it right, eventually and after quite a heated discussion, but we wouldn't trust him at all.

We stayed one night in a standard room and one in a deluxe room. The standard room - ground floor - is only metres away from the path to the dining room and so, unless we drew the curtains shutting out the views and fresh air, we were constantly being observed by guests on their way to eat or walking to their rooms. The deluxe room was on the floor above, in a different building, and did offer some privacy. Rooms were certainly in need of updating - old furniture, tired and dull bed covers and decorations. Carpet felt decidedly dirty. 
We ate dinner in the hotel's restaurant the first night but were so disappointed with the food, that we ventured into town and ate at Cafe Concerto the second night (a 15 minute walk and well worth it). Breakfast was again just average. Two complaints. First if you come to Pokhara for trekking, as we did, the trekking companies want to get on the road as early as possible - 7 am - but breakfast doesn't start until 7 am- If so many tourists are here for the trekking, why not open the restaurant at 6:30 to accommodate them? And second, timing of the items coming from the kitchen - you can have toast at 7 am but butter didn't arrive until 7:20; coffee and cereal were in place when we arrived at 7 am, but milk took considerably longer. While all the staff were friendly and courteous, they need training in efficiency and organization. 
Grounds - another reviewer mentioned this - were attractive and if you have a clear morning, the view of snow capped mountains is a wonderful way to start the day. A new restaurant is under construction and that constant hammering and drilling (until 9 pm) spoiled the experience for us but once complete, I imagine this would be a very peaceful place away from the hustle and bustle of the town (although only a short boat ride and short walk away).

The garden was first developed as a private venture in 1920. It was subsequently taken over by the government but fell into disrepair until the Austrian government sponsored renewal of the gardens early in the 21st century. The redesign was pioneered by a German architect Gotz Hagmuller who also still owns the Milla Guest House in Bhaktapur (where we stayed).
It is now around half its original size and there is a small museum that contains photos illustrating its original layout. The gardens themselves are immaculate and there is a café, Kaiser Cafe, named after the original owner that looks out over the garden. You do need to pay the entrance fee to gain access to this.
It provides welcome respite from the frenetic activity outside the tall walls that surround the garden.

Soaltee Crown in Kathmandu is beautifully and expansively located covering a huge area with good restaurants, a casino, and lush green gardens with a picturesque view of mountains in the background.  The hotel itself is beautifully decorated with traditional woodwork.  Its a pity that the combination of such a beautiful location and so much land under a prestigious hotel brand does not make up for some of the downsides of the hotel, which with a little more attention can be completely overhauled.  First of all, the rooms in some wings are damp and dark which gives them a certain shabby feel.  I stayed in June and since it was raining it was making it feel even more damp and gloomy.  The room amenities such as toilets and showers needed a retouch and fixing and these were not looked into till I started staying in the room.  The carpetings and upholstery didn't help the feel if not worsened.  I felt that for the price I was paying I wasn't getting as comfortable an accomodation.  I also felt that the hotel didn't utilize the acres of green it had under its wing properly as during my two weeks stay I didn't see much use of the outdoors other than to lounge around.  The hotel can do so much better by organizing outdoor bar-b-q's, open air entertainments etc.  This is especially needed for a hotel like Soaltee since it is a bit of a ride from the more happening areas of the city such as Thamel. 
The plus sides of the hotel are its friendly staff who demonstrated a nack for personal attention and the wonderful restaurants, specially the Chinese restaurant it has under its roof.  The other restaurants had great food too and so did room service.

review:
This hotel is a classic from back when people were only starting to go to Nepal, but it hasn't really been renovated since 1970. It is on it's own island on the lake right next to the town of Pokhara, an transport to and from the hotel is done via a barge that his pulled by an attendant using a fixed rope to either shore. While this is kind of cool at first, it takes a while and gets old rather quickly. 

The rooms facing the lake are festooned with plaques commemorating the stays of various prime ministers, UN Secretaries General, Prince Charles, and Jimmy Carter. All of these too place in the 60's and 70's. It is telling that none has taken place since. The rooms are incredibly small and have two single beds with blankets and sheets that could be described as "adequate." The bathrooms are an afterthought that are crammed into the center of the circular buildings so that all bathroom windows open onto a small center space and you can be treated to the sounds of your neighbors in the bathroom every morning. Showers have hot water, but that's about all I can say for them. Rooms generally feel like a weird room form a US National Park Service lodge at a third-tier national park from 1980. 

This is not to understate the convenience of the lodge as a base for seeing the surrounding area or the beauty of the lodge's location. The sun sets in back of the lodge so that they Annapurnas across the lake are lit up with the colors of the sunset and are reflected in the lake on a calm day. An amazing view and one to which semi-professional photographers flocked. From Pokhara you can walk anywhere you want in the Annapurnas, including to Annapurna base camp if you have a week each way. But the options are limitless. 

Be aware that Winter in Nepal is the dry season, so the cities are socked in with smog. The first day we were there, we couldn't see the mountains because the smog was so thick. However, if you spend a little energy to hike into the hills to the North, you can get above / beyond the smog, and then the views of the Annapurnas is amazing. I'm not too sure what the other hotel options in Pokhara are, but I go tthe sense that they are all fairly low end. All in all this is probably one of the better options in the area. 

The town of Pokhara itself is overly touristy. Restaurants are good and the presence of so many tourists ensures that picky eaters from the West can find a pizza or pasta, but I don't consider this a plus. The town is full of tourist traps with rip off North Face and the same stuff as everybody else. Generally I would stay out of town and spend my time in the hills.

Also, do upgrade to the superior room. Our second stay, the room was much bigger and nicer as we were upgraded to a suite of some sort with a sitting area. This second stay was 3 stars, so I ended up giving 3 stars on this review. 2.5 would be more accurate.

We were finishing up a long holiday with a few days in Kathmandu and wanted to have a mini splurge. Unfortunately whilst Kathmandu is chockful of backpacker digs, there really are not many good midrange options. After blanching at paying a lot of money for what looked like a very average Radisson we stumbled across the Shanker and thought we would give it a try.
We managed to negotiate a free upgrade from a standard room to a suite. Oddly however, the standard rooms may actually be nicer than the suites; the suite had a lot of dead space which we did not use and, because of its size, was not particularly cosy (which is key in somewhere quite chilly like Kathmandu). Wifi is passable (although not free unless you negotiate it) but annoyingly you could only use it on one device at a time and had to continuously keep re-logging in. The hot water was good but you have to wait a good couple of hours between showers to get hot water throughout. 
The hotel has a certain charm, with Rana wood carvings everywhere but the whole thing has a slightly old fashioned, musty air. Breakfast was distinctly average (slash poor). Service varied; the people cleaning the rooms were very helpful but the food serving staff (especially around the pool) were patchy.
All in all the Shanker is an enigma of a hotel but we would still be inclined to recommend it above its peers in Kathmandu (but largely because it is a very poorly serviced class).

Had visited this underground cave in Pokhara a long back ago. This cave is sacred to the Hindus and is a popular tourist attraction.

Background: As part of a two-week escorted tour of India and Nepal, our group passed by the Gupteshwor Mahadev Cave in Pokhara. At approx. 8,500 feet, it is said to be the longest cave in Nepal.

PROS: Located near the town centre along Siddhartha Highway, it's easily accessible. It is just across the street from Devi's Fall that the two can be combined in one 2-hour trip (or half-day if including a hike from the World Peace Stupa). Technically, it is an easy-grade cave. The main shaft is nearly horizontal in nature, no side branches, not requiring SRT (single-rope technique) training or any extra special gear of any kind, in-cave navigation is very simple, the path is lit, no ladder pitches, easy to access from the surface, and is a short trip of less than one hour, well suitable for the complete beginner. 

CONS: To be clear, this is NOT a cave for spelunking (cave exploration). It is set up more as a Hindu shrine and a tourist attraction. And my use of the term "attraction" is already quite a stretch. Before the ticket booth are numerous souvenir stalls selling overpriced wares. There are no cave guides, but you can just follow the endless procession of people ahead of you. After descending a wide spiral staircase, you will enter the cave to find it dark, damp and dingy. Whatever illumination you find is provided by a sparsely strung-out series of small, dim light bulbs. As you inch past the Cow Shed, you reach one of two chambers. This main one is dedicated to the Hindu god Shiva; it has a large stalagmite which resembles (or is symbolic of) the deity. Watchful guards forbid photography here. And if you wish to pay your respects to Shiva up close, you'll have to line up, remove your footwear, step on poop or what-have-you, and walk barefoot up to the shrine. (No, thanks!) Now, past the shrine is the cave's second section, where you gingerly inch forward over uneven slippery rocks plus a slippery single-lane metal staircase to see the bottom part of Devi's Fall. This section is often crowded and is closed during the rainy monsoon due to flooding.

Verdict: It goes without saying that, if something is not worth seeing, it is not worth visiting. And having to pay NRs100 for foreigners, it feels like a rip-off. Not unless you're a devout Hindu or feeling mightily philanthrophic, in which case, be my guest. Don't get me wrong but, with all due respect, no thanks. Grade C-minus.

This is one of the world’s largest stupas and home to a large Tibetan Buddhist community in the city.  Admission is 400 rupees payable as you approach the main square. On reaching the stupa, the first thing you see are crowds of people all walking clockwise around the perimeter. It is important to walk in this direction as this is a sign of respect. Access is also allowed on the first tier; shoes must be removed. Here devotees are prostrate in prayer, the whole experience is very moving
Good time to visit is late afternoon when a colourful ceremony occurs near the Ajuma shrine. Gifts of rice, sweets, biscuits and money are handed to Buddhist monks, the food is placed in a large vessel and mixed together while one monk recites scriptures and others playing various wind instruments creating a solemn atmosphere.  The food is then placed into bags and at the end of the ceremony, handed to devotees as gifts.
Aside from the temple, there are shops and restaurants all around the site, there were huge crowds in the square at the time of our visit and the atmosphere was palpable. A memorable experience.

review: I stayed at the Soultee 3 nights as part of a guided trek in the Everest region.  We were supposed to stay 4 nights (2 before the trek, 2 after) but we got stuck in Lukla thanks to poor weather.  I had been to Kathmandu 25 years ago and stayed at what was then considered one of the best hotels (the Malla) - but was surprised at the poor water and electricity outages there back then.  I was very glad to find that the Soultee was definitely up to par - good water (although we were told to only drink bottled) and great electricity/internet.  The hotel provided extensive glass-bottled water and was doing an excellent job recycling glass and not adding to the extensive plastic problem.  The rooms were very nice and very quiet, all looking out onto this huge private courtyard/gardens that were very well maintained (the hotel sits on 12 high-security acres and there are many other buildings - like a full spa and casino).  The beds were very comfortable and I enjoyed great nights of sleep.  The breakfast was extremely good - I especially liked the many different lassi drinks and yogurt, the fruit drinks, the bakery items, and the Indian fare (e.g. pakoras, ginger chutney, and masala/chai tea).

Quaint architectural entrance with spiral steps featuring murals of shiva-parvati on the walls that lead down to the mouth of the cave. Inside the cave the first feature you will note is the underground temple dedicated to Lord Shiva (correct me if I am wrong). Signs indicating 'No Photography' apply only to the temple, not the rest of the cave.

Steep and slippery steps through the cave follow down through small tunnels (you may need to bend over if you are tall, and those with weak knees beware). The tunnels are often wet from water dripping from ceilings and on the floor (so don't wear your best clothes and shoes). At the time of our visit construction works were ongoing so expect a lot of scaffolding and pipes in your way. At the end of the cave you can see the Davis waterfall flowing into the underground river.

After the visit you could walk across the road opposite the entrance to the cave and enter the park above ground (pay separately) that has a limited view of the Davis waterfall from the surface.

Worthwhile to experience a taste of Nepal underground.

review:
Like all hotels in Nepal - you will be sold the fact that Prince Charles of the UK once stayed here amongst many other celebrities. But that was over 25years ago - an it appears no money has been spent on this hotel since. The flowers surrounding the garden in this place and the lake view are pretty, and the ferry man takes you over to the small island upon which the hotel sits. You can hire a rowing boat (extra charge and row your beloved out across the lake to see the mountains) But the illusion of comfort ends there! - the hotel rooms themselves - are very damp (and in my opinion as an asthmatic were dangerous to my health as they contain spores of fungi and bacteria.) The blankets on the beds are damp and the rooms themselves were constructed of painted hardboard - and the rooms very tiny. The shower being a tiny room with black mould in the crevices. We were initially not provided with a kettle or tea making facilities and told that this would be an extra $50US per day - we were paying around $130!USDollars. In Nepal - the hoteliers have no idea of Western Hotel standards and have every intention of charging over the odds for poor facilities and bad service and generally ripping off tourists. The Restaurant food was buffet style and represented very poor value for money being barely edible. The swimming pool was smaller than my duckpond, dirty with missing tiles and generally useless. The hotel ads show you viewing the mountains from this pool - which was impossible when we were there in April 2013. The employees at the hotel seem to be having a better time than the guests, I smelt dope being smoked by one of the gardeners!
So that my health didn't deteriorate we checked out after two days and continued our stay at the Pokhara Grand Hotel - which gave us a huge suite with a view of the Annapurna Mountain range from our windows - they also offered more reasonable trips, microlight flights and paragliding all at cheaper rates than those offered at Fish Tail.  All hotels in Nepal are effected by poor hot water supply and poor electricity supply - so you can expect to be stuck in lifts and eating of using the bathroom in the dark at random times during the day. Sadly I have nothing good to say about Fish Tail - it needs bulldozing and rebuilding again! Its surviving on past memories of glory when it was probably the only hotel in Pokhara!

The Crowne Plaza Soaltee.

This is a grand hotel with many rooms. In Kathmandu  There is a huge lobby.  The staff is competent.  However, while we were waiting in the clearly marked No Smoking lounge an Arab in full regalia sat down and lit a cigar at a table clearly marked No Smoking and the staff brought him an ashtray!  

Food in the buffet dining room is always divided between vegetarian and non vegetarian or local and western.  The food is of good quality.  Wifi access is by fee only and is pretty expensive.  There is no free zone in the lobby as in many hotels.  A local beer is more than 250% than can be obtained in local restaurants.  This is gouging.  

I have no idea of room costs here as we were assigned by our tour, however, wifi policies would tell me to not return.

If you do come however, accept a room whose numbers run from 01 to 37, preceded by the floor number.  Eg, 416 is room 16 on the 4th floor.  These rooms are in the newer wing and are better equipped electrically for recharging.  Other room numbers higher than these are in an older wing, which, according to us, smelt of damp, plus one definitely needed an adapter.

Let me begin my review with the positives -
1. Very warm and friendly staff
2. Rooms are spacious and are maintained neat & tidy
3. Bathrooms are very clean
4. There are 4 restaurants in this property and all of them are good! Especially in the one which serves buffet breakfast, you tell the staff your food preferences on day 1 and they will remember it during your entire stay duration and no need to repeat it :)
5. Room service is really quick and efficient

On the flip side -
1. After a couple of hours delay in landing at Kathmandu [not blaming the hotel for this ;) ], the courteous hotel staff with your name board calls the driver and your approx. 45 min. to 1 hour journey to the hotel begins! Within a few minutes, you realize that on a hot, sunny, smoky (due to vehicle pollution) afternoon, the taxi AC's won't be switch ON as hotel as instructed their drivers so. Even after insisting that it is getting really nauseating, the driver still not turn it ON and then you call up the hotel and literally explain it a few times (coz they will keep transferring the call, for reasons better known to them) then the driver would obey their command! I haven't faced it in any other part of the world. May be it is a norm in Kathmandu and people who frequently travel to Kathmandu are accustomed to this. But, I wasn't :(. Hotel was kind enough to waive off the airport pick-up bill and also upgraded me to a next higher level room type.
2. As if my tryst with the cab wasn't enough, in the upgraded room allotted to me on the club floor, within half an hour of check-in water started dripping near the wardrobe and I had to get myself changed to another room. Later on I learnt it was due to some issue with the air conditioner that the water was dripping. Isn't it the hotels responsibility to look after these aspects before allotting rooms to guests?
3. On the last nights of my 3N stay at about 4:30 AM some strange nose (as if someone is hammering or driving a screw) started and it was growing louder and louder to disturb the sleep. After I switched ON the lights and started searching for the source of the noise it gradually stopped. After the initial fantastic experiences, I didn't even bother to report this to the hotel staff.

To sum up it was a one-off experience . . .!

General Information:
Due to the after effects of the earthquake many places in Kathmandu are still undergoing redevelopment works and this hotel is also in such a phase. I saw that the pool wasn't yet available for use and some construction work happening almost round the clock.

My suggestions to the hotel management is to put the correct rating for the Hotel and also urgently look into the cleanliness and restoration of this heritage hotel which has great potential but flatters to deceive.

After walking through the roadside archway, before entering the cave, there are many souvenir stalls.  Before the ticket counter is a round concrete balcony which allows a close look at the cave entrance and the statues leading up to it.  After the ticket counter, enter down the large spiral staircase.  Here there are many modern statues and plaster works depicting semi-clad ladies to bearded men similar to some of the Kathmandu Valley's erotic carvings.
As you enter the cave you'll discover how dark it is inside.  The lighting is a series of small light bulbs so a torch comes in handy.  As you descend a little, you will see a small tunnel like cow shed.  About 40 meters further down is the main Shiva temple.  No photography is allowed here.
The lingam is enclosed in heavy iron grills.

- No peep hole on the room door. 
- Front desk staff were found sleeping on the couch at 5am every morning. However there was security guide at the main entrance. 
- Dinner at the restaurant was almost double the prize for the quality you can get from Thamel.

I stayed in this lovely hotel overnight, before trekking into the Annapurna Region with my guide. 
The grounds are beautiful, though I didn't see much of them, as it is December, and I quickly huddled into the lobby after being dropped off by the taxi driver.
The staff are polite and old world class. 
The room was a little dank and dark, and cold, until the heat kicked on. 
You could tell this was the off season. I went down for breakfast, which was free with the room stay, and the only other people in the cavernous restaurant area (I almost want to call it a banquet  hall) were two Chinese businessmen visiting from Xian. 
The food came out bit by bit, and finally I had to go. 
Not a bucket list hotel. but worth visiting in Nepal.

Boudhanath, also known as Boudha, is one of the most significant Buddhist sites in Kathmandu, Nepal, and indeed, one of the largest stupas in the world. This ancient monument stands as a symbol of peace, harmony, and enlightenment, encapsulating the essence of Buddhist philosophy and practice.

The origins of Boudhanath date back to the 5th century AD, although its precise founding remains shrouded in legend and myth. According to tradition, the site was established by the Lichhavi King Manadeva after a dream in which the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara instructed him to build a stupa at the location. Over the centuries, Boudhanath has undergone several renovations and expansions, becoming the impressive structure that it is today.

At the heart of Boudhanath is its magnificent stupa, a massive hemispherical dome adorned with intricate carvings, prayer flags, and colorful prayer wheels. The stupa is surrounded by a circular path known as the kora, where pilgrims and visitors alike walk clockwise, spinning prayer wheels and reciting mantras as they circumambulate the sacred monument.

The significance of Boudhanath extends beyond its architectural grandeur. It serves as a focal point for Buddhist practitioners from around the world, attracting devotees, monks, and scholars who come to pay homage, meditate, and engage in religious rituals. The bustling streets surrounding the stupa are lined with monasteries, temples, and shops selling religious artifacts, creating a vibrant atmosphere of spiritual devotion.

One of the most striking features of Boudhanath is the piercing gaze of the all-seeing eyes painted on the four sides of the stupa's tower. These eyes, known as the "eyes of the Buddha," are believed to symbolize wisdom, compassion, and the ability to see beyond the material world.

Boudhanath also plays a significant role in the cultural and social fabric of Nepal. It serves as a gathering place for festivals, ceremonies, and cultural events, bringing together people of diverse backgrounds in celebration of their shared heritage and beliefs.

In 2015, Boudhanath suffered extensive damage during a devastating earthquake that struck Nepal. However, through the collective efforts of local communities, international organizations, and government agencies, the stupa was meticulously restored to its former glory, reaffirming its status as a beacon of hope and resilience in the face of adversity.

In conclusion, Boudhanath stands as a testament to the enduring legacy of Buddhism and the power of sacred architecture to inspire and uplift the human spirit. Its majestic presence continues to draw pilgrims and seekers alike, offering a sanctuary of peace and enlightenment in an ever-changing world.

review: Pokhara is famous for mountain views and lakes but underground there is a hidden secret - the spectacular Gupteswar cave. The cave is well worth a visit for those interested in geology as the cave is linked to the Devi Falls across the road, and to the lake and to the mountains.  You might think the entrance to cave is set in a rural landscape, but it is easy to miss unless you know what you are looking for. The entrance is through an archway almost hidden in busy shops along a busy road. Walk through the entrance arch and along a few metres through market stalls to the ticket office - the entrance fee is very small for tourists.  Also time your visit to the cave for days other than the local Saturday holiday or any other public holiday otherwise you will be surprised to find hundreds of locals visiting the cave making it very crowded. The entrance is quite amazing as in the middle of the shops and market stalls you walk down a deep staircase into the dark cave which is only lit by lightbulbs strung along the roof. Highly recommended you take a torchlight. Then follow the stairs as fair as you can go first through the main cave and then deeper underground to a huge cavern - the view is spectacular as you can see daylight shining through an opening in the rocks where the Devi waterfall across the road pours into. During the monsoon season this deeper cave may be closed due to the amount of water pouring in. The Gupteswar Cave is said to be one of the longest and deepest in south east Asia, and you can only marvel at the size and depth of the cave and its link to the river and the lake and up to the mountains. Allow about 2 hours for the visit. It is not suitable for people who do not like enclosed spaces as you need to walk through a very narrow tunnel to reach the big cave and the path is wet and slippery - but there is plenty of fresh air in the cave coming from the opening where the waterfall comes into the cave. And when you come out of the cave and look across the road to the Devi Falls, you can only wonder how the cave has manage to survive as above it are roads, traffic, shops and cafes and busy city life!  Well worth a visit.

review:
I had a very bad experience in this hotel (Barahi Pokhara) compared to its other two sister establishments Barahi Chitwan and Sarangkot Mountain Lodge. I would like to thank Sagar from Barahi Chitwan and Roshan from Sarangkot Mountain Lodge for their outstanding service and hospitality during our stay.
Though, Barahi Pokhara being it's main company, seems like they have forgotten what hospitality is. I had a bad experience from the moment I landed at Pokhara airport. We were expecting hotel staff to welcome us at the airport gate as we had paid for the service. Yet, no sign of any staff. I called the number provided to us during the reservation. To my dismay, I was advised by the chauffeur to go to the airport car parking area and look for him. 
Moreover, when we reached the hotel reception, they did not seem to have our itinerary briefed. They did not know anything about our honeymoon package itinerary that we specially booked and paid for. The hotel manager accepted that there had been an internal miscommunication. I was clearly not happy about all the proceedings. I did not expect this type of mistake from an establishment who claims to maintain and provide high standard service to its guests.
We were shown our room and to my surprise or should I say my biggest disappointment, there was no decoration. The decoration, we had paid an extra for. The room we booked was a deluxe room but it was just an ordinary room. All our honeymoon euphoria was drained. Disappointed and disgusted by the service provided. I did not get what I paid for. I complained to the hotel manager about what had gone wrong with the arrangement the hotel had arranged as it doesn't match with our honeymoon package we had booked for. I expected a quick fix. Nothing was followed up until after 2 hours I had to chase the hotel manager. All I heard from him was,"I am sorry and I will fix it up in 15 minutes. 
I told the hotel manager that we were going out and asked him to make an arrangement as per our honeymoon package and expect that all is fixed when we return.
It was our honeymoon trip and it was ruined from the beginning. There was no goodwill gesture from the hotel even after this horrible experience. 
I hope the hotel will not repeat the same mistake again and not ruin someone's special trip.

There was also a fountain where visitors are encouraged to toss in coins for good luck. There are always young entrepreneurs at Nepali sites with fountains who are eager to sell coins to visitors!

Right at the end of the cave is a very limited amount of space (about 10 people max) to stand and view the falling water through the gap between the rocks. The cave walls just before the iron stairs have some sort of white mineral deposit of them, which was interesting to see.

I really wanted to like this hotel.  This was my first time to Nepal on business, and I booked this hotel based on the uniqueness of the property and it's relatively good location to Thamel and some other key spots.  The out side of the hotel and lobby are pretty and historic, however once in the room, everything is outdated and a bit dirty.

Pros:
-Good location
-Friendly/helpful staff

Cons:
-Extremely hard bed, slept horribly through entire stay
-Terrible internet connection throughout the hotel.  Nearly dial-up speed in the guestrooms.  Furthermore, the connection resets every single day, so you have to retype the access codes for all your devices individually each day.  And the internet is around $8 per day, so I expected better for the price.  It's especially frustrating trying to do business from the hotel.
-The breakfast buffet was awful and made me feel nauseous every morning.  Nothing seemed extremely fresh, even the fruit.
-None of the rooms have views.

All in all, you kind of get what you pay for.  I would have much preferred to pay more for a better stay in Kathmandu.

Just completed a three nights stay at this hotel as a delegate to a conference held at the hotel.

The journey from airport to hotel was about half hour, the journey from hotel to airport...on a Sunday morning...took over an hour; through chaotic streets.

The hotel is over a large area. Several well maintained greens. Furniture indicated it was probably constructed in the 80s when heavy wood and brass were much used just hotel furnishings. That's absolutely fine, but very disappointed with housekeeping:
1. My minibar fridge had moulds growing!
2. Cigarette ash and crumbs of food under my bed, very easily visible from the sofa.
3. One of the towels had brown stains.
4. Bed post and table tops were not dusted properly.
5. Don't think top of sofa back had ever been dusted!!
6. Sachets of tea/coffee/sugar in the room were kept in haphazard manner.

I mainly had room service food. Food quality was ok; not much sign of quality, but I got the impression they tried their best with the limited supply of quality ingredients or imported goods.

The staff were warm and friendly. Whoever attended to me...from reception to bell desk to room service people...were helpful. They seemed to really try, that's more than many brands more luxurious than Crowne Plaza.

I understand options are limited in Kathmandu, so one might not have much of a choice. If one has "appropriate" expectations from this property, one will be just fine.

review:
I just came back from Kathmandu today and I would like to complain about your reception staff Binod Khanal.

As a cabin crew, we are given the chance to stay at your hotel with free breakfast and free internet inside the crew lounge. However, everytime I check-in these layover hotels I prefer to have my own internet connection in the room even if I have to pay for it. What I didn't like though was that I was charged twice in 1 day for 24hour usage of this wifi.

Money is never a problem for me. What upsets me most was that your staff, Mr. Khanal, was very hostile and unaccommodating to this issue. I asked him why I have been charged twice when our stay was even less than 24 hours. He said that the procedure is that you will be charged for every device that you use to connect to the internet. I told him I was not informed about this and it wasn't even stated at your hotel's website. I used both my laptop and my iphone to connect to the internet. He simply dismissed it by saying that this is how it's always been and he said he'll just forward it to the management. This staff didn't even show any concern at all and he was really rude. He even told me smugly, "you should've just used the crew lounge."

Having heard this, I simply gave him my credit card instead of the cash that I was holding which was amounting to how much I thought my bill was in Nepalese Rupee. He swiped my card and punched in the bill total of NPR 4325.64 ( NPR1360 charged twice for the 24hour internet, NPR950 for room service minus NPR190 crew discount, plus service charge and 13%VAT). He didn't even try to comprehend how unreasonable the situation was. He wasn't even facing me properly that's why I wasn't able to get his complete name. I was really upset with how disrespectful he has been.

Another thing, around an hour before I checked out I decided to avail the free breakfast buffet in the hotel. In the middle of breakfast, everyone could hear one of the guests shouting in front of the reception area and I saw where that man was standing: In front of exactly the same spot I was in when I checked out, most probably in front of the very same staff I'm complaining about.

Working before as a front desk receptionist, I am familiar with the hotel system and I know that he could have done something else to pacify me as a guest. He could have emphatized with me at the very least. Perhaps being a crew member did not earn me any respect since we were staying at your hotel for a discounted rate unlike other paying guests.

All in all I could say your hotel has improved as compared from my last stay, especially the Garden Terrace breakfast buffet. However, this incident has dampened what could have been a much better layover. I hope you can do something about your internet policy and I certainly hope you could give your receptionist some advice on how to treat your guest properly.

Boudhanath Stupa is a must-see when visiting Kathmandu. It's one of the largest stupas in the world, and the spiritual energy here is truly mesmerizing. As you walk around the stupa, you can see pilgrims spinning prayer wheels, monks chanting, and people from all over the world taking in the peaceful atmosphere.

The stupa itself is beautiful, with its iconic white dome, eyes of Buddha, and colorful prayer flags fluttering in the wind. I recommend visiting early in the morning or around sunset when the atmosphere is calm, and the stupa is beautifully lit. It’s a great place to meditate, reflect, or simply enjoy the moment.

There are also several rooftop cafes around the area, offering a great view of the stupa while you sip on a cup of tea. You can easily spend a few hours here, soaking in the serenity and exploring the small shops that sell Tibetan artifacts, prayer flags, and souvenirs.

The first time I visited Devi's falls it was right at the height of monsoon (indeed it was raining when we went) and I was amazed!  This MASSIVE flow of water rushing straight at us, and then... POOF!  it disappeared down a big hole.  my friends and I spent some time wandering around for different view points to see where the water went.

The second time I had talked it up so much to some friends they were all buzzed, and then quite disappointed.  We came in May, at the end of the long dry season, and there was barely a trickle of water coming down the canyon (although now I could see the canyon itself, which was also interesting, geologically) and then going down a big black hole.  Interesting, but hardly mind-blowing.  the lack of water also revealed a lot of trash hung up on the rocks and plants surrounding the cave, which definitely took away from the mystique.  For a dry-season cave experience I recommend the Bat cave as my favorite natural attraction near Pokhara (some of the caves are closed during monsoon because of the water levels).

We (3 Couples) went to Nepal for a leisurely experience for 5days and 4 Nights. We stayed at Soaltee for 3 Nights, and 1 Night at Nagarkot. Coming back to the Crown Plaza,

1) Check - In : 
It was smooth, but despite informing them beforehand to arrange for better rooms (mountain facing), they gave us back facing rooms on 2nd Floor which had views of a pathetic terrace with generators. 
2) Welcome Drink : 
Pathetic. Which 5* property in this age serve you Lemon and Orange Squashes for welcome drink? At least have some courtesy to serve Juices instead of Squashes after paying 7K INR a night.
3) Rooms : 
As I mentioned earlier, we were given the worst kind of rooms on 2nd floor. Rooms weren't clean. There were hairs all around on the Bed linen and on Washroom floor. Bed was comfortable though. Television wasn't working in one of the rooms which they repaired after complaining. I think they are on a cost cutting spree, as if you want to get the linen changed, you need to leave a placard on the bed. There weren't any Tooth Brushes / Shaving Kits nothing inside on the wash basin. On the next day, after a lot of fight with their duty managers, they changed our rooms to 3rd floor and 5th floor, which had better views and were nicely maintained.
4) Food : 
- Breakfast - Excellent. Had a wide spread from Indian, Continental etc.
- Dinner - Had Dinner at Garden Terrace. Both Food and Service were pathetic. Food, especially the Paneer dishes were stale (which we complained to the chef also). Service was pretty slow.
- Room Service - Was fast, but again the quality of food was bad, looking at the price.
5) Swimming Pool :
It wasn't operational. The reason they cited was maintenance, but after confirming with some other people, it was actually a marriage which forced the shut down of the pool. A engagement ceremony took place besides the pool. The management was actually fooling the people residing to accommodate this function. Frankly speaking, we choose this Hotel because of its Pool, but we really felt bad at the attitude of management at the hotel.
6) Gym / Sauna / Steam Bath :
Excellent. All 3 facilities were nice and properly maintained. The staff at the male Sauna section were great and friendly, but the ladies complained about the behavior of some staff at the Female section.
7) Service / Attitude :
This was the biggest problem with this hotel. Since, its a big property, no single person is responsible for the maintenance. I would especially like to mention the name of their Duty Manager, Mr Deepak, to whom we complained about everything. Instead of helping us, he didn't listen to us, rather was rude and unaccommodating. He didn't even let us meet the senior management, rather said that he's the senior most guy available. 
The service Manager of Garden terrace was good though. 
8) Check Out :
Check was fast and quick.
9) Casino :
Nice and excellent. People present there really helped us understand the games, and kick start.

Overall, its a big property with lots of people staying in their Hotel. Its basically a business hotel, booked mainly by Travel agents. I would highly recommend to converse with them about the rooms, recreational facilities etc before checking in. Our stay at the property was pretty average looking at the price we paid.

This is the biggest Stupa in Kathmandu and can be considered an entire town by my standards. I went there hoping to experience Buddha though I am a non-believer as in my country there is nothing close to this. 

Indeed this is probably the best-maintained stupa. However, if you do not believe in paying the entrance fee (because it often does not lead to maintenance), walk around to the area where all the public buses congregate (towards Ratna which is the closest public stop to Thamel as Thamel itself is a tourist district and controlled differently)  outside, the locals have a way to enter and exit freely without a gantry. Just follow the locals.

Inside, there are tonnes of restaurants, but most are rated poorly on TA. We went to a decent cafe and indeed, it was overpriced and underwhelming. Inside the Stupa, it is just a place for monks to meditate. Everything is extremely dusty and covered in webs, the only thing that sparkled is probably the gold statues which cannot tarnish. 

If you go there to pray you may get what you ask for, but as a tourist, a few pictures from the outside sufficed. (no photos permitted inside anyway)

*Hot showers with strong water pressure to rinse off the dust of Kathmandu.
*Bottomless high-quality coffee in the breakfast hall every morning.

Not so good:
*Breakfast buffet was all fairly tasteless even with many options available.
*Standard size room is a bit too small to be really comfortable.
*Somewhat difficult walk to get to where the action is in Thamel.

Overall, a fine place to stay if you are looking for a hotel with some history as well as decent amenities in central Kathmandu.

Stayed for 2 nights, 1st morning (where we get up early to catch the sunrise) do not have hot water for washing up.

The hotel has charm. It's has intricate paintings and woodwork everywhere. You can tell someone built this property with the intent to make it the best around.

Sadly that's no longer the case. But wait, there's more....

The hotel is just fine. No more, no less. If you have traveled to India, Pakistan, Bangladesh before.... This hotel will be great. If you've never been to this part of the world, you'll be wondering how nobody has noticed the gaps in the grout lines in the bathrooms.

The hotel indeed has charm and the makings of its former glory. I suspect it needs a manager that has experience in western hotels to bring it back. The staff try, and some even try hard but like most things in this part of the world... They miss the mark.

That all being said, we enjoyed our stay here. It's far away from the Hustle and bustle of the street. That's a positive and a negative. If you decide you don't want to eat at the hotel restaurant, you'll have a 5-10 minute walk minimum to an alternative. The hotel restaurants food was surprisingly amazing. Well the Indian fare at least. Food prices were reasonable for Nepalese rupee. Service could be better, but they try.

The grounds were quite nice and well maintained. The hotel itself is majestic from the outside. I would stay here again because it's good value for the money and the cleanliness rating is above par for this part of the world. It's quiet for this part of town. Walkable to areas like thamel. We were also comped wifi... Nice touch.

My message to the manager of this property: there is an American TV series named 'hotel impossible' buy, download do whatever you can to obtain it. This is the easiest way, I think, to learn about western standards for service and cleanliness. Hotel shanker could be one of the best hotels, if not the best hotel in Kathmandu if they learned some simple standards from western hotels. For instance, have at least two people at the lobby desk at all times. Never let them leave that post. If something is needed let them call someone to come take care of the problem. The second issue - clean the chandelier above the restaurant entrance. It's disugstingly dusty. Lastly, the restaurant staff need to be proactive in filling water and ensuring all placements are present. Lose the bamboo placemats, they trap food.

review:
Fishtail Lodge markets itself as a top range hotel/resort offering the best views of the lake and Annapurna range in Pokhara. Three standard rooms are marked as having special views and are sold at a premium - we stayed in one of these (Room 16) on our honeymoon. The room normally has two single beds and although the offer was made to push the beds together, we said that we would prefer not take the room. The hotel then promised to put in a double bed for us as we were staying for four nights. We booked on that basis. On arrival, the room had two single beds pushed together. We asked for the double bed to be put in but this didn't happen.

The room promised unobstructed views. In reality, there is a grass area in front of the rooms that is open to all hotel guests with chairs and hammocks. We found our views were often of other guests  relaxing or taking photographs of the view or each other. Some guests seemed to enjoy peering in our windows too - when they weren't climbing through the flowerbeds to get better camera angles. The area in front of our rooms also seemed to be a social club for hotel staff to come and chat (shout to one another) or have conversations on their mobile phones. This also spoilt the tranquility somewhat. 

The restaurant served very expensive food that was really pretty grotty. Mostly bland international fare - even the Nepali dishes were bad. One, for example, turned out to be fish and chips despite an exotic description. The breakfast buffet was exorbitant, especially when the only food taken were a couple of slices of bread and some undercooked potatoes. There is no atmosphere in the restaurant either, with the only diners seeming to be large tour parties on corporate rates. This is a missed opportunity as the views from the restaurant were great. But better to eat in town.

The location is mercifully quiet but access to town is by a raft or rowing boat and then through a bus park. This makes a trip into town quite time consuming and after a couple of days the novelty does wear off. At night, the approach road and bus park are very dark which can be intimidating. 

Oh, and the wonderful view was mostly obscured by clouds - don't bank on being able to see the mountains. 

All in all, this is probably the best hotel in a town where most offerings are loud and garish. But it is still not quite hitting the spot, despite charging top dollar Western prices.

I waited to catch a waiter's eye to mention the roach was still alive, but before I could - another staff member scooped it up and threw it out in a napkin.

I appreciate the service they are going for - but it was a bit too much. We could barely have a conversation without someone approaching the table and doing something. They said there was no way we should have been told it was a tax. Basically, the wait staff took advantage of 'new forigners' and ended up with a 25% tip. Not impressed at all.

I would go back to the hotel, as it was fantastic, but I would not eat at their Indian Restaurant again.

review:
When we were asked by people at Kathmandu where we were going to stay for two nights at
Pokhara and we replied that it would be at The Fishtail Lodge, they said that we'll be staying at
a very fine property and one of the best in pokhara. Once featured in the book 1000 places to
visit before you die, this picturesque resort managed by the Annapurna hotel was once the prime
vacation spot for famous people including Prince Charles. Thus with high hopes we proceed to
FTL.
Getting to the resort is actually fun and gets you into the mood of staying with nature. You
require a boat or a raft to get from the roadside to the resort as we have to cross a part of the
gorgeous phewa lake. The staff manning the rafts were very friendly people. The raft service is
available 24×7 as that is the only way to reach the resort.
The only downside to this setup is that during the rains there is a good chance that some of your
luggage may get slightly wet as was our case. But the staff were really careful.
The resort itself is breathtaking and beautiful. Since it is literally in the lake, you get a
wonderful view of the Himalayas beyond it. However since we visited during the monsoon season
we could only see some distant hills due to the low clouds. Nonetheless, it was still beautiful.
It's quite, secluded and peaceful. The resort is laid out in the form of many cottages with each
cottage having a couple of rooms. The main building had the lobby and the restaurant called The
Circle which also has a bar. The lobby had a board with pictures of all the celebrity who have
stayed here. We were checked in quickly and taken to our two rooms which were attached.
This is where the resort started disappointing us. The rooms at one glance were clean enough
and in good shape although a bit small. But the lack of maintenance supervision showed as we
started using the rooms. To say the least, they were in a very bad state. To start with, one
bulb in each of the rooms weren't working. This room had severe lack of lighting when it's the
evening and the handful of warm bulbs don't actually brighten up the room much. Add to that
broken bulbs, then it was almost hard to read books. There were no table lamps or bedside lamps
either which, to be honest, is very poor for a resort that is said to be the best at Pokhara. The
windows couldn't lock properly as the locks were bent and deformed. The TV reception was poor
and seeing the TV properly was almost impossible. The cables and even the receiver were just
hanging out of the TV with no support. The numbers on the keypad on the phone were almost
completely wiped out and barely visible. It shows that the phone is very old and hasn't been
properly maintained. The coasters for the cup were very filthy and stained. The cups were also
dirty and we had to clean one ourselves. The slippers provided in the room in our cupboard was
used as there was sand on it. These may be small things but they show how badly kept this place
is. No wonder the amount of celebrities visiting this place lately has been less. The photos have
been attached below.
After keeping our bags in the room, we went to the restaurant to have some snacks as we
hadn't eaten anything since morning at it was about 4. Since it was rainy they provided umbrellas
for us to walk to the restaurant. The restaurant was cozy and warm with a fire place at the
centre. There was also a large screen showing the cricket world cup matches. It also has a bar.
The main dining area is further down with views of the beautiful phewa lake. Outdoor seating
is also available. Our server showed us to our table and presented the high tea menu and the all
day dining limited menu. We ordered a plate of veg pakoras, grilled veg sandwich, grilled cheese
sandwich and some hot and sour soup. The food was excellent. Really good quality and tasty with
a sizeable quantity.

We left for our rooms and after refreshing ourselves and resting for a while we went to have
dinner back to the restaurant. Again, we were shown to our seats and given the dinner menu.
We had some Indian dinner which was also great. The one slight complaint that I felt was that
the restaurant staff, although they were extremely friendly, weren't polished.
Breakfast the next day, was in the form of a buffet having various Indian, Chinese and
Continental options. Everything was great except the sambhar which didn't even taste like
sambhar. Otherwise the spread was big and really good.
After breakfast we went for the city tour of Pokhara and came back before dinner. We had light
dinner of various snacks as we were full from the late and heavy lunch. Again, the food was
good.
The next morning we explored a bit around the resort as the rains had stopped. The resort
as I mentioned above was beautiful and it also has a pool. We went for breakfast but was
disappointed that there was no buffet due to the lack of customers there. Instead we could
order food in an à la carte format. The selection was huge and maybe even more than the buffet.
We had a little of everything in the Indian selection and some noodles. All of it was good, except
the sambhar. We ordered a bottle of water to drink because we don't prefer the normal water.
As we were about to leave the restaurant we were presented with a bill. I was confused because
the breakfast was complimentary. When I checked the bill, I found out that they charged me
for the water bottle! Usually at buffet breakfasts bottled water is complimentary. Never have
I been charged extra for mineral water for a buffet anywhere where I've stayed across the
world. I don't mind paying for it, and I did because that may be the policy here (but I'd argue that
it is a very weird one). They could've atleast told us that it was chargeable when we ordered it
instead of surprising us with a bill in the end! That was very unprofessional.
We went back to our rooms to pack as we were checking out that morning. Before we went we
called the manager and showed him all the problems in the room. He took it well and accepted it
as positive criticism. He said he was sorry and that it was unacceptable that the rooms were
in this state. He was very friendly. I appreciate the time he took to hear me out and to accept
their mistakes. I've had many instances at other places where such criticism wasn't taken well,
but the manager was extremely professional.
Upon departure, the hotel staff presented us with some souvenir. They gave the women a
handmade pouch with some jewellery and the they gave the men the traditional hat.
The only reason I gave this place 2 stars is mainly because of the friendly staff and the good
food. The rooms were horrible.
I also stayed at the Annapurna Hotel at Kathmandu and I found that this lodge had identical
problems. The rooms were poor but the staff and food were excellent. So is this because of a
lack of supervision by the officials at the Annapurna group? Maybe. But whatever is the case the
renovation and maintenance of the rooms are well overdue.
I do not recommend staying here from my experience.

The short - For 30npr it is beautiful and powerful waterfall especially after heavy rain or monsoon season. And accessible by public bus from Pohkara.

-------

Having only 3 stars on TripAdvisor I believe this is a harsh review. After monsoon season or heavy rain it is beautifully powerful and spectacular to see. You can't see the bottom of the falls but you can see the top section and still sense how much force there is.

It is located opposite the cave on the other side of the road it is a short bus journey from Pokhara (catch a green public bus from the main bus station on the main road and ask to stop at Devi's Fall and it'll cost about 30npr pp each way). 

Entrance is through a massive orange sign that says Davis Fall. Walk through the little stall to the ticket counter. Entrance cost 30npr pp - try to use small change as they don't always have change available.

Walk through the entrance on your right and proceed straight on to see a high up view of the waterfall. Take the steps to your right to go down to get a closer look.

There is fencing all around the waterfall and is safe to visit. There are also toilets available to use inside the area on your right as you first walk in.

review: Known as Nepal’s most famous cave, it is located just across the street from Devi’s Falls. Said to be discovered in the 16th century, it may be the longest cave in Nepal at 9600 feet (2950 m). The cave is venerated for its huge stalagmite worshipped as a Shiva lingam. To enter the cave, you’ll pass through a shopping arcade and then down a spiral staircase lined with carvings and statues. Things go downhill (literally) after that. The inside of the cave is damp from the continual dripping of water. The floor is wet and slippery; thankfully there are handrails down the steps. While the cave has lighting, have you own light handy just in case. You’ll need to watch your head in several tight places. If you’re claustrophobic, this is not for you. Eventually you’ll find yourself in a damp cavern. A sliver in the rocks provides a view of Devi’s Falls (5 stars)! Overall, the experience didn’t feel safe and I was anxious to get out of the cave (1 star). The water from the falls forms an underground tunnel, under (or around) and though the cave. During monsoon season this part of the cave may be closed.

Outside the complex, there are shops selling handicrafts, clothes etc. The entry fee is a small fee. One can visit the Gupteshwor Mahadev Cave located close by.

In Nepalese language "Patale Chhango" means underground waterfall. It is aptly called so because its water mysteriously vanishes underground. It reportedly goes in the Gupteshwar Mahadeo cave which is also quite deep down under nearby.
The waterfall has three levels and the tourism department of Nepal has constructed good steps, galleries and bridges to view its glory. The wate to this fall comes from Phewa lake overflow.
We visited the fall in April and hence the fall was thinner. But it must be great view just after the monsoon.
I also spotted a pair bird called Blue whistling thrush near the waterfall.

review: I stayed here as part of Friendly Planet's Taj Mahal Express tour with Nepal extension. This hotel has a good location and beautiful grounds, but inside was outdated. There is also a casino on site. It was definitely not "hopping" with people, but we just played at our own table and had the opportunity to talk to the locals working there. There are several dining options in the hotel, and the food was decent, but several items on the menu were not available. The pool area is lovely and was a nice place to spend the morning before the flight home. This hotel has the potential if it updated its interior, but our tour guide did mention that Friendly Planet was no longer going to use this hotel as either a Hyatt or a Hilton had recently been updated.

Let me start off by saying that I believe that on another occasion in another part of this big hotel, things might have been a lot better. 

We met with a large group of friends (500 of us) arriving at the hotel mainly over a period of 2 days. Reception was clearly not prepared and did a really lousy job at trying to get everybody checked in as fast as possible. Personally I had 3 people staying in line before me, which should not have been so bad, especially taking into account that everybody was pre-registered and that all dues were paid in advance. Novertheless, I had to wait 25 minutes. 

3 counters, 4 hotel employees who could actually check you in, and at least 6 trainees that tried to make copies of passports and were getting in the each others way. After checking your payment, we were transferred to another person who checked your passport, then off to a person who was supposed to block an amount on your creditcard but actually charged it, to finally get the the person who gave you your key card. What a mess!

My room was situated on the ground floor. The water in the toilet reached 2 cm under the toilet seat. I called reception who sent a plumber right away. He showed me a trick to get the water to a normal level. It consisted in having to flush 3 times, each time you would use the toilet. Afraid every single time everything might just overspill during the process... 

I had to wait 3 hours and call reception twice to get my Wifi connection going.

The AC worked perfectly well. 

The closet doors didn't fit in the wall perfectly and were very difficult to open or close. 

The room had a good view on the front lawn of the hotel.

Second night I woke up to set foot on a completely wet carpet. Water sipped from under my door (no idea where it came from, but it was a very rainy night). Again, service arrived quickly, and used tens of towels to try dry everything. Eventually, the next night, everything got back to normal, except for a bad stench in the room, that lingered on until I left. At no time did anybody suggest I should get another room.

When I wanted to extend my stay for one more night, I was offered a price that was 40 dollars more expensive then a reservation I was able to make through Booking.com on the same day. Only after seriously complaining and asking for the manager, did they agree to do something for me.

As we were in a group, some meals were included, others were not. We had badges, and each time we went to a restaurant that was not in charge of serving us our included meals, we were stopped. Each time we had to explain that we understood this, and that we would pay separately for our food. Apparently very difficult to grasp...

The wake-up service worked fine. 

The conference rooms were well equipped but the AC took time to kick in.

The party halls were very nice.

The hotel bars were not prepared for the number of guests and run out of soft drinks, run out of ice, and even run out of some alcohol also resulting in long waiting times.

In general the staff was not very friendly. It seemed like they were stressed out by the large number of active guests. It showed. It was not very professional. 

Again: although I'm sure that under other circumstances things would have been much better, this was a really bad stay. 

Won't be back here!

review:
Unique Cave Experience in Pokhara — Worth a Quick Visit

We visited Gupteshwar Gupha, one of Pokhara’s well-known cave temples. The entrance is small, and you’ll need to walk down a narrow staircase to enter the cave. Inside, it’s a bit dark, slippery, and humid — so good footwear is a must.

The natural rock formations are interesting, and you’ll find a Shiva Lingam temple inside, which adds to the spiritual feel of the place. As you walk deeper, you can also see a glimpse of Devi’s Falls from inside the cave, which is a unique viewpoint.

It’s a short visit — around 20-30 minutes — and worth seeing if you enjoy caves or spiritual sites. However, those uncomfortable with narrow, damp, and uneven paths might want to skip it.

Overall, a decent and different experience in Pokhara for a quick stop.

review:
I need to preface this review by telling you that we had just come off a 17 day trek, a trek that we weren't ready for ending- we wanted to keep going but you dont know that when you make your original plans and we had planned to finish our trek in Jomsom and fly to Pokhara. So, my review is possibly not as enthusiastic as it might have been if we had been ready for it.
Anyway, arrived early morning after a flight from Jomsom. To the hotel's credit early check in was not an issue. 
The room was high floor and facing into the hotel grounds. The porter assured us that next time we could get a lake view- it hadnt occurred to me to even request one, so if you want a lake view pre-request. We were happy with our view of the gardens.
The room was big, light and had a great little balcony.
Furnishings, bedding and walls need a spruce up- they are looking dated. Same with the bathroom.
Bed was comfortable, sheets nice and clean and the a/c was useful in quickly cooling the room down. Quiet nights sleeps, we didnt hear noise for other rooms at all. The bathroom was very functional, deep bath, hot water (luxury) and enough amenities provided.
Used the restaurant for breakfast only. It was always busy but we managed a seat inside. Outside  diners seemed to be having problems with flys. Breakfast food was fine- fruit, porridge, cereal and some hot Nepali and international dishes. Bakery items were plentiful. The wait staff did a great job at keeping your cup of tea/coffee refilled and they were very pleasant. WIFI available here.
There is a coffee shop with wifi too, big range of baked goods and a very nice cup of coffee (first one for weeks).
Big pool- lots of people enjoying it and it looked lovely.
Location works- close to restaurants and the main shopping strip.
Checkout efficient.
In conclusion, it was fine. Would I stay there again- no, I didnt "fit" the hotel. I'd go smaller and more personal.

Poor wifi signal in my room which made it very difficult to have Skype calls back home or for work. Wifi seemed to work fine in the lobby with a strong signal.

Probably one of the WORST gyms I have frequented at all IHG hotels. It's small, poorly equipped, no ventilation, poorly lit and worst of all, wooden floor which makes equipment such as bench slide. Location
Not much around but then again, it wasn't that far by taxi to anywhere in Kathmandu unless there's traffic. Dining option outside of the hotel is very limited and mainly just local Nepali food.

Breakfast
Limited choice but the staff working at the restaurant was so nice and efficient. Really appreciate the morning coffee as well as the take away coffee that was generous prepared for me every morning.

Overall, a suitable hotel for a long business trip. However rating downgraded due to the extremely poor gym facility - hugely disappointing. Fantastic staff though who were always willing to help.

I'd read the reviews for Fishtail before leaving, so I kind of knew what to expect, but it doesn't stop you still being a bit disappointed by the whole experience. 
The management and staff at Fishtail seem to live of this air that it's an exclusive resort that we are all lucky to be staying at with the (yawn) heritage of all their famous guests. Well look carefully people, when was the last time you had anyone rich, famous or powerful staying there?? According to your own proud posters, about 25 years ago (if you exclude Betty Boothroyd's visit in 1994). So yes, about 25 years ago, which to my reckoning, should be when the place was refurbished and cleaned up, cos it certainly hasn't been since then!!!
To be fair though, there was some refurbishment work going on in the two story building when we were there.
Out two night stay there was part of our honeymoon. We actually spoke to reception and mentioned it was our honeymoon and could we upgrade to one of the lake view rooms. By the way, we hadn't asked for a free upgrade, if it was reasonable we might have considered it. The guy on reception didn't even acknowledge anything we had just told him, and just gave us this long spiel about how these were the rooms that the dignitaries stayed in (yes we know, yawn) and therefore bound to be at least twice the rate we were paying. To be honest, we didn't even pursue it after that, this guy was so far up his own ****side we couldn't be bothered!
 I have to be honest, overall this is the most unwelcoming and unfriendly reception I have ever come across.
We were shown to our room, where all the doors and windows were wide open, we walked in and it stank of damp. The smell seemed to go when we put the a/c on but as there were so many power cuts it was a constant battle. 
Apart from that, and the obvious need for a refurb, it was ok. We had neighbours on both sides and didn't hear them so I guess it was well insulated! 
The hotel restaurant buffet and a la carte menus were pretty basic and the food quality was mediocre. We had much better, cheaper and more authentic food when we ventured out over the road / lake. Didn't try the spa, but my husband used the pool a couple of times to cool off and said it was nice. 
The grounds of the hotel and its location are really the best and only things going for Fishtail Lodge. I guess, because of that they don't have a lot of competition. But really, up your game Fishtail, you could be such an amazing place to stay.

Every time I visit Pokhara, I do visit Devi's Fall too. Nepal, being rich in it's season, every time you visit you will see different view of Devi's Fall due to the season change. In summer, or in rainy season there'll be abundance amount of water while in winter or off season water'll be in it's lowest (March). 
Devi's Fall is also known as 'Patale Jhango' in Nepali.

The in-room wifi was okay, when it worked. It frequently didn't work. It would drop out and not come back on for hours, or it would drop in and out making work impossible and browsing a frustrating experience.
The other thing was the noise. I was just unlucky with the room, I guess, but considering I was one of the first at the conference to book in, they should have given me a better room and left mine empty or at least the last assigned. It was right above the diesel generator and since the power frequently went out it would start and stop often. It was uncomfortably loud.
To be fair I was approached by hotel staff each morning at breakfast and asked how everything was. When I complained about the noise they suggested I could go to reception and asked for a different room. I had already unpacked for a week stay and didn't want to be bothered re-packing to relocate. I regretted that more and more as the week progressed.
Finally, this hotel is a fair way from anything. It is a big compound that has a few shops, but no convenience store. So it was quite a walk to go to the shop for snacks or anything.
On the plus side, my room was one that has been renovated recently and the bathroom was good. Great shower actually. The room was not large, but big enough. The bed was comfortable.

Hotel Shanker is located in an old colonial building about 10-15 minutes walk from Thamel. While situated nicely - away from the noise of Thamel, it is let down by the service.

- The Hotel in a guarded and gated compound so safety is pretty good. However, when walking back from Thamel at night, you will need to stay alert as you need to cross two busy roads.

- Service was a let down at the hotel. Check in staff were unhelpful and unfriendly.

- The rooms were large and clean but nothing exceptional. USB ports and universal power sockets were available which was a plus. Otherwise, the furniture and decor were functional but tired looking. 

- Wifi was available in the room. Speed was slow during peak times - breakfast and night.

- Breakfast was available each morning in a large dining hall. An egg station was available but was not particularly interesting. The highlight however were the different curries served each morning. 

- An outdoor pool is available - but unheated. Though perfectly fine after a day of walking the streets and temples.

- Typically, I don't go to the hotel restaurant for dinner. However, rather than crossing the busy roads at night, we stayed for dinner for one night. Food was good, though it was more Indian than Nepalese. The room service menu was different and significantly cheaper than the restaurant. If the weather is good, recommend having the room service meal delivered to you by the poolside.

Overall, the hotel is basic (by Western standards) and provides some sanctuary after a day of walking around the city. If the service improved, it would be even better.

review:
Devi's Fall is well known amongst the locals and tourists. Costs NPR 30 (20 for Nepalese citizens) to enter the site that has been poorly maintained (plastic bottles and rubbish every where). Does it worth NPR 30? I let you be the judge. It is not a huge fall: if you were expecting a Fall like Niagara, you'd definitely be disappointed. Go without any expectations.

Regardless, it is one of the point-of-interest in Pokhara. Your Pokhara visit cant be complete without visiting Devi's Fall.

It is said that Devi fell in the gorge and so it was called Devi's Fall.

If you prefer, follow these:

1. Take a short stroll along the lake side road (towards Basundhara Park) and go to Dam Side Park (ask locals how you can walk there) (15-20 mins walk). Cost: a coffee or cigarette for yourself.

2. Once you're done at the Dam Side Park, get out of the park, cross the road and wave at the next bus. Ask if the bus goes to Devi's Fall (some people also call it David Fall)

3. Get in the bus and ask the bus conductor to stop you near Devi's Fall. (Cost: NPR 30).

4. Once off the bus, look for the "Welcome to Devi's Fall" sign across the road. Go through little alley (entry cost: NPR 20 for Nepalese citizens, NPR 30 for all others).

5. Once you exit Devi's Fall and you're back on the road, cross the road and go to your right (say around 100yards/meters) and you will see the entrance to Mahendra Cave and Guptshwar Mahadev. Follow the signs: they are in English too (entry cost: NPR 10 for Nepalese citizens, NPR 30 for all others. If you see Kamadhenu cow as well, it is optional, it will cost additional NPR 10)

6. Once you're out on the road, go towards your left for about 250yards/meters where you can catch buses to the World Peace Pagoda (costs up to NPR 100). Ask the locals if you can't find the bus stand (there are no signs). No, don't walk to the Stupa unless you're in a big group. Walk is scenic but QUIET (less travelled) and steep. You never know what kind of people you may encounter on the way. Be safe than sorry!

7. Once out of the Stupa, catch a cab (costs NPR 800; 1000 max) to Lake side!

Voila!
